title: Only formed faith actually justifies; unformed may be called justifying as disposition
source_text: XIX. Haec est ergo communis doctrina Scholae Romanae solam quidem fidem formatam & vivam actu justificare, sed tamen fidem, etiam quum nondum formata est, esse dispositionem quandam ad justificationem, & hoc respectu quoque posse justificantem dici, nempe per modum dispositionis necessariae & praerequisitae, quanquam, nisi alia accedant, inutilis maneat, nec ullum actu justificet. Inter se vero non omnino consentiunt quomodo sint interpretanda illa Paulinarum Epistolarum loca, ubi toties affirmat & contendit Apostolus hominem justificari fide, ex fide, & per fidem. Et multi quidem existimant Paulum ibi per fidem intelligere illam quae viva atque formata est, & mentem ejus esse, nos coram Deo reddi, ac haberi justos per fidem illam quae per dilectionem operatur. Alii vero putant Paulum ibi fidem absolute sumere, & prout abstrahit a fide tum viva, tum mortua; & sensum ejus esse, fidem esse primam & maxime necessariam dispositionem ad justitiam consequendam, hominemque per fidem disponi ad justificationem, & sine fide non posse ad eam pervenire. Quam utramque sententiam refert, nec improbat Thomas Stapletonus citato libr. 8. de Justif. cap. 16. & 17.
pass_a_gloss: This then is the common Roman doctrine: that only formed and living faith actually justifies, yet faith even when not yet formed is a certain disposition toward justification, and in that respect can also be called justifying, namely by way of a necessary and prerequisite disposition, although unless other things are added it remains useless and actually justifies no one. They do not fully agree how to interpret those places in Paul letters where the Apostle so often affirms that a person is justified by faith, from faith, and through faith. Many think Paul there means living and formed faith, and that his mind is that we are made and held just before God by that faith which works through love. Others think Paul takes faith absolutely there, abstracting from living and dead faith alike, and that his sense is that faith is the first and most necessary disposition for obtaining justice, that a person is disposed to justification by faith, and that without faith one cannot arrive at it. Stapleton reports both views and does not reject either (De Justif. 8.16-17).
pass_b_english: Common Roman teaching: only formed living faith actually justifies; yet not-yet-formed faith is still a necessary prerequisite disposition and may be called justifying in that preparatory sense, though alone it remains useless and justifies no one.

On Paul justified by, from, and through faith, some Romans read living formed faith working through love; others take faith absolutely as the first disposition without which justification cannot be reached. Stapleton records both without rejecting either (De Justif. 8.16-17).
